opus-5.5.text:
I think they're going to be incredibly varied, probably more than most people imagine. We tend to picture "the robot" as one thing, usually a humanoid, because that's what science fiction gave us. But when you look at what the work actually requires, the form should follow the function.

At one end you'll have very small, specialized machines: robots that crawl inside pipes, inspect turbine blades, work in tight spaces in a data center, or even operate at a medical scale inside the body. At the other end you'll have large systems for construction, mining, agriculture, and logistics, machines that move tons of material and run around the clock. In between there's a huge middle ground of mobile manipulators: a base, an arm, some good sensors, built to handle the messy, semi-structured tasks in warehouses, hospitals, retail, and the home.

Capabilities will vary just as much. Some robots will stay narrow on purpose. They do one job extremely reliably and cheaply, and that's exactly what the customer wants. Others will become much more general because of advances in AI, especially foundation models that let a robot understand instructions, perceive its environment, and adapt to things it hasn't seen before. That's the big shift right now. The intelligence is becoming somewhat portable across bodies, so you can put a similar "brain" into very different hardware.

So I don't see the future converging on one dominant form factor. It looks more like the vehicle world: we have scooters, sedans, pickup trucks, eighteen-wheelers, forklifts, and nobody expects one design to replace all of them. Robots will be the same. There will be a whole ecosystem of shapes and sizes, each tuned to the economics and physics of a particular job. The common thread will be the software layer that makes them easier to deploy, easier to teach, and safer to work alongside people.

r001.rationale: The response compares robots’ variety to the vehicle world, listing vehicles from scooters to eighteen-wheelers, and says robots will likewise span an ecosystem of shapes and sizes.

fable-5.1.text:
I think they'll be incredibly varied, and honestly that's the part people underestimate. When most folks hear "robot" they picture one of two things: a humanoid walking around a warehouse, or a robot arm bolted to a factory floor. But that's a bit like looking at computing in 1975 and only imagining mainframes.

What we're actually going to see is a whole ecosystem. On the small end, you'll have things the size of a shoebox or smaller doing inspection work inside pipes, crawling through HVAC systems, maybe moving inventory around on a shelf. On the large end, you'll have autonomous machines the size of a truck doing earthwork, agriculture, mining, things where the payload and the environment demand mass and power. And in between you get everything from delivery platforms to mobile manipulators in hospitals to legged systems that can handle stairs and rough terrain.

The reason I'm confident about that spread is that the hard part is becoming shared. For a long time every robot was a bespoke engineering project, where the perception, the control, and the software stack all had to be built from scratch for that one form factor. Now you've got common perception models, common learning approaches, and increasingly common hardware components. Once the "brain" is reusable, the body becomes a design choice driven by the task rather than by what's technically possible. That's when you get diversity.

The humanoid gets a lot of attention, and I understand why, because the world is built for human bodies. But I'd push back on the idea that it's the end state. It's one shape among many. If you're moving pallets, you don't want two legs. If you're inspecting a bridge cable, you want something that can climb. The best form factor is the one that fits the job, and there are a lot of jobs.

So my honest answer is: more varied than most people expect, and probably more boring-looking than the science fiction version. A lot of the most valuable robots over the next decade are going to look like appliances, not androids.

r001.rationale: It predicts wide size variation, from shoebox-sized or smaller robots to truck-sized machines, with many sizes in between.

astra-6.text:
I think we’re going to see a huge variety, because the size and shape of a robot really ought to follow the job it’s doing. A robot that’s inspecting a pipe is going to look very different from one moving pallets in a warehouse or helping someone in their home.

There’s a lot of attention on humanoids, and that makes sense—we’ve built our world around people. But you don’t need two arms and two legs for every task. Sometimes you need wheels, sometimes you need something very small, and sometimes you need a big, powerful machine.

The exciting part is that very different robots can share capabilities in how they perceive their surroundings and make decisions. So I’d expect a broad range of specialized bodies, with increasingly capable intelligence behind them.

r001.rationale: The response predicts a broad range of robot sizes, from very small to big, but does not compare that range to the variety of vehicle sizes seen on roads.

sol-6.1.text: I think they’re going to be incredibly varied. We tend to picture a robot as a humanoid, but the right shape and size really depend on the job. A robot inspecting a pipe is going to look very different from one moving pallets in a warehouse or helping someone in their home. You’ll have small, specialized machines and larger robots that can do a range of tasks. The key is matching the capabilities to the problem: what does it need to sense, how does it need to move, and what does it need to manipulate? I don’t think there’s going to be one form that wins across all of those environments.

r001.rationale: The response predicts substantial variation, from small specialized machines to larger robots, but does not compare that range to the variety of vehicle sizes seen on roads.
